To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) the in group bias is a strong phenomenon in bullying episodes, and 2) the in group is more protected from bullying when it is the victimized group.

1) the in-group bias was stronger in the victimized group than in the bully group, 2) the in-group favoritism was more pronounced in boys than in girls, 3) the manipulation of teacher's likability did not affect participants' perception of inter-group aggression, 4) girls attributed a higher degree of punishment to both groups than boys did, 5) the attribution of punishment was higher in the victimized groups than in the bully groups.

students' perception of the bullying episode was influenced by group membership (in-group bias) and by gender (boys accepted physical bullying more easily than girls did), while the manipulation of teacher's likeability was not effective.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social processes that underlie bullying, and the role of group membership and social identity in students' perception and evaluation of a bullying episode.

the social processes that underlie bullying episodes and with how students' perception and evaluation of bullying might be influenced by the context and the group membership of the victim and the bully.
the role of group membership as a determinant of students' perception of aggression at school.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
bullying is a social phenomenon that involves a number of variables, both individual (gender, age, etc.) and group (in group vs. out group, group size, etc.) related.
the social process of bullying is influenced by the group membership and by the gender of the participants.
the group membership and the social context in which bullying occurs are important factors in the perception of bullying.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the group dynamics of bullying can be influenced by the social context and by gender.
group membership and teacher likeability affect adolescents' perception of bullying in a social context.
group dynamics and pre-adolescent social concerns play a role in how adolescents perceive bullying.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the social dynamics involved in bullying episodes are not restricted to the dyadic level, but are influenced by the context and by social group variables.
group identity is a key variable in understanding bullying as a social phenomenon.

group dynamics play a key role in the perception of a bullying incident, and that students' perception of the event is not only affected by the roles they assume, but also by other variables, such as the teacher's likeability.
